s: Theseus was driven from Athens by Menestheus after Heracles had sent him there.
A spiral shell carried by Minos in his search becomes a reward challenge when threaded, enabling him to discover Daedalus was with Cocalus.

passes_through spiral shell [drawn by an ant] Daedalus fastened a thread to an ant and allowed it to pass through a hole bored in the spiral shell. Minos found the thread passed through the shell and inferred that Daedalus was concealed with Cocalus.

l: Minos’s pursuit of Daedalus, The Library
s: Minos pursues Daedalus through different countries, using a spiral-shell test that leads to Camicus, where Cocalus’s ruse kills him after he finds Daedalus’s hiding place.

l: Cocalus’s ruse with the shell, The Library
s: Cocalus receives Minos’s spiral shell and gives it to Daedalus to thread; Daedalus uses an ant and thread, completing the task but revealing his presence to Minos.
Minos's death occurred at Cocalus's court after Cocalus promised to surrender Daedalus and entertained him. The daughters of Cocalus killed Minos by pouring boiling pitch over him while he bathed.
Boiling pitch was poured over Minos by the daughters of Cocalus while he bathed, and it killed him.

Hippolyte, also called Glauce and Melanippe, was mother of Hippolytus. Armed with Amazons at Phaedra’s wedding, she threatened Theseus’s guests and died in the ensuing battle, under differing accounts.

Demophon, child of Celeus and younger brother of Triptolemus, was the infant Demeter tried to make immortal on the fire. He later married Phyllis, received her kingdom, left her promising to return, settled in Cyprus, and died after opening Mother Rhea’s casket and falling on his sword when his horse stumbled.

l: false accusation against Hippolytus, The Library
s: Phaedra made a false accusation against Hippolytus after fearing that he would report her advances to Theseus. She tore open the doors of her chamber and her clothing to support the accusation, and Theseus believed her.
Hippolytus died after his horses were frightened by a bull sent from the sea. His chariot was dashed to pieces, and he was dragged to death after becoming entangled in the reins.

Ixion, father of Pirithous, falls in love with Hera and attempts to force or violate her. Zeus tests and deludes him with a cloud resembling Hera; Ixion boasts of enjoying her favours, then is punished, bound to a wheel and whirled through the air by winds.
carries Ixion [through the air, driven by winds] The wheel was the instrument of Ixion’s punishment. Ixion was bound to it and carried through the air by winds.
is_a daughter of Oenomaus Hippodamia was the daughter of Oenomaus. She fell in love with Pelops when she saw his beauty and persuaded Myrtilus to help him in the marriage contest.

is_attended_by centaurs [as Hippodamia’s kinsmen] At the wedding of Pirithous and Hippodamia, the centaurs were feasted as her kinsmen. They became drunk and attempted to violate the bride, leading Pirithous and Theseus to fight them.

l: battle between the Lapiths and centaurs, The Library
s: includes Caeneus [as an invulnerable fighter] The battle occurred at the wedding of Pirithous and Hippodamia after the centaurs attempted to violate the bride. Pirithous and Theseus fought the centaurs, and Theseus killed many of them.

wrote Troilus [a play referring to the marriage] Sophocles referred to the marriage of Peleus and Thetis as voiceless or silent in Troilus. A fragment attributed to him also says that Thetis deserted Peleus because she was reproached by him.

Helen’s abduction includes Theseus and Pirithous taking the twelve-year-old from Sparta; later the Dioscuri carried her away with Aethra. Alexander then persuaded her to leave Sparta while Menelaus was in Crete, taking property, and her rape marked the war’s chronology, with Greeks preparing in year two.
is_a capture The Dioscuri, together with the Lacedaemonians and Arcadians, captured Athens. They carried away Helen and Aethra, while Demophon and Acamas fled.

l: return and enthronement of Menestheus, The Library
s: is_a return and enthronement The Dioscuri brought Menestheus back and gave him the sovereignty of Athens.

l: descent of Theseus and Pirithous into Hades, The Library
s: is_a descent Theseus and Pirithous descended into Hades while seeking marriage with Persephone for Pirithous.
is_a deception Hades deceived Theseus and Pirithous by pretending that they would partake of good cheer and instructing them first to sit on the Chair of Forgetfulness.
is_associated_with Lethe The Chair of Forgetfulness was where Hades told Theseus and Pirithous to sit. They grew attached to it and were held fast by coils of serpents.

l: binding of Theseus and Pirithous, The Library
s: is_a binding [by coils of serpents to the Chair of Forgetfulness] Theseus and Pirithous became attached to the Chair of Forgetfulness and were held fast by coils of serpents. Pirithous remained bound forever, while Theseus was brought up by Heracles.
is_a rescue [by Heracles from Hades] Heracles rescued Theseus from Hades and sent him to Athens.

Tantalus is a king and Niobe’s father. He reveals divine mysteries to men and tries to share ambrosia, then is punished in Hades: standing in a lake beneath a hanging stone beside fruit trees. Another record calls him Thyestes’ son, Clytaemnestra’s former husband, and Agamemnon’s victim.

A punishment in Hades perpetually confines Tantalus in a lake beneath an overhanging stone: water reaching his jaws dries when he tries to drink, while winds lift nearby fruit trees to the clouds when he tries to eat.
Broteas is a hunter who does not honor Artemis, claims fire cannot harm him, becomes mad, and dies by throwing himself into fire.

Fire is a valuable substance, often first possessed or withheld by a deity, animal, bird, or other supernatural being. It reaches people through theft or recovery: Beaver steals it from the Sky people, brings glowing coals after rain extinguishes fire on earth, and fire is made on earth for the first time by the Lame Boy. Its transfer explains its continuing presence in trees, wood, and stones, from which it can be elicited by friction, boring, rubbing sticks, or striking stones. Once obtained, it lets Earth people keep warm in the upper air, enables the mechanical arts, and is preserved for later use. In legend and custom, it also serves Demeter’s attempted gift of immortality and protects, purifies, gives courage, or removes fairy changelings when children pass over, around, or through fire or smoke.
is_ruled_by Oenomaus [as king] Pisa was the kingdom ruled by Oenomaus.
Suitors of Hippodamia enter a marriage contest, carrying her by chariot toward the Isthmus of Corinth as Oenomaus pursues; he kills those overtaken, reportedly twelve, displaying their severed heads.

l: chariot-race for the suitors of Hippodamia, The Library
s: A chariot race in which a suitor flees with Hippodamia while Oenomaus pursues in armor; reaching the Corinthian Isthmus wins Hippodamia’s hand in marriage.

Myrtilus, son of Hermes and charioteer of Oenomaus, loves Hippodamia and sabotages Oenomaus’s chariot by omitting linchpins, causing Oenomaus to lose; dying, Oenomaus curses him and wishes Pelops to kill him.

is_caused_by Pelops [according to some accounts] Myrtilus’s failure to insert the linchpins caused Oenomaus to become entangled in the reins and be dragged to death. According to another account, Pelops killed Oenomaus.

Thyestes, a Pelopid and father of Aglaus, Callileon, and Orchomenus, initially rules Mycenae after using Aerope’s golden lamb, but the sun’s reversal confirms Atreus’s claim. Banished after swearing at Hera’s altar, he is fed his sons’ cooked bodies by Atreus. An oracle directs him to father Aegisthus with his daughter for revenge; Aegisthus kills Atreus, restoring Thyestes until Agamemnon and Menelaus exile him to Cytheria.
Aerope, Atreus’s wife and Catreus’s daughter, loves Thyestes, commits adultery with him, and gives him the golden lamb.

Aegisthus, born from Thyestes’ union with his daughter, learns his parentage at manhood, kills Atreus, and restores Thyestes’ kingdom. He later joins Clytaemnestra in murdering Agamemnon and Cassandra, rules Mycenae, and is killed by Orestes.

The Peloponnese was formerly called Apia and was inhabited by Pelasgians. It was conquered by the Heraclids, who were first defeated and later finally conquered it; it was also associated with the rule of Tisamenus and with the exile of Laius.
Mycenaeans receive an oracle, then send for Atreus and Thyestes to choose a Pelopid king for Mycenae.
A golden lamb, born in a flock, appears after a vow, is hidden then given away, and determines Mycenae’s kingdom through Thyestes’ claim.

The Sun is a deity with cattle on Thrinacia, a palace, and a chariot used daily. It reverses its course and sets in the east, establishing Atreus’s claim to rule after Thyestes’s agreement. When Ulysses’s companions slaughter its cattle, it reports them to Zeus. It acknowledges Phaethon as its son and reluctantly lets him drive the chariot; a similar son in Indian accounts causes destructive heat.
The Mycenaeans seek a Pelopid to rule the kingdom. Thyestes first receives it through the golden lamb, but Atreus takes it after the sun reverses its course; Aegisthus later restores it to Thyestes.
The oracle tells the Mycenaeans to choose a Pelopid as king, leading them to summon Atreus and Thyestes.

l: Atreus and Thyestes’ contest for the kingdom, The Library
s: Atreus and Thyestes dispute who should rule the kingdom. Thyestes claims that the owner of the golden lamb should be king, but after the sun reverses its course, Atreus takes the kingdom and banishes Thyestes.

l: reversal of the sun, The Library
s: The reversal of the sun’s course occurs after Thyestes agrees to make it the condition for Atreus’s rule. It serves as a divine indication that Thyestes has acted improperly and that Atreus should receive the kingdom.

l: Aerope’s adultery with Thyestes, The Library
s: is_a adultery Aerope, who is married to Atreus, commits adultery with Thyestes and gives him the golden lamb.

l: murder of Thyestes’ sons, The Library
s: is_committed_by Atreus [after luring Thyestes by a pretence of friendship] Atreus lures Thyestes with a false offer of reconciliation and kills Thyestes’ sons, Aglaus, Callileon, and Orchomenus, after they seek refuge as suppliants at the altar of Zeus.

is_a cannibalistic meal [Thyestes unknowingly eats his sons] Atreus cuts up and cooks Thyestes’ sons and serves them to Thyestes without their extremities. After Thyestes has eaten, Atreus reveals the extremities.
is_caused_by Atreus After the sun reverses its course and Atreus takes the kingdom, Atreus banishes Thyestes from the country.

l: Aegisthus’ killing of Atreus, The Library
s: Aegisthus, after learning that he is Thyestes’ son, kills Atreus and restores the kingdom to Thyestes. Aegisthus killed Atreus after learning that he was Thyestes’s son, and he restored the kingdom to Thyestes.

is_cursed_by Myrtilus The house of Pelops is represented here through the conflict among Pelops’s sons Atreus and Thyestes, the adultery of Aerope, the murder of Thyestes’ sons, and the later killing of Atreus by Aegisthus.
rescues rescue of Agamemnon and Menelaus [from the killing of Atreus] The nurse took Agamemnon and Menelaus away after Atreus’s death and brought them to Polyphides in Sicyon.
Polyphides ruled Sicyon, received Agamemnon and Menelaus, and later sent them to Oeneus.
Aetolian king of Calydon who received Agamemnon and Menelaus after Polyphides sent them to him.
is_betrothed_to Neoptolemus [previously, in Troy] Hermione was Orestes’s wife and had previously been betrothed to Neoptolemus in Troy. When Orestes went mad, Neoptolemus took her.

Orestes is raised in Phocis by Strophius alongside Pylades. After consulting the god at Delphi, he avenges Agamemnon by killing Clytaemnestra and Aegisthus, then is pursued by Furies, suffers madness, and is acquitted at the Areopagus when the votes are equal. He later receives another oracle, travels to the Taurians, and escapes with Iphigenia and a wooden image. In the principal account he marries Hermione and fathers Tisamenus; another account names Erigone. He is said to kill Neoptolemus and ultimately dies from a snakebite at Oresteum.

Iphigenia is brought to Aulis under a false promise of marriage to Achilles; Artemis carries her away and substitutes a deer. As a Taurian priestess, she recognizes Orestes and Pylades and escapes with Orestes carrying the wooden image; some accounts make her immortal.

Palamedes, son of Nauplius and Clymene, exposes Odysseus’s feigned madness by threatening Telemachus, forcing Odysseus to reveal himself. Later, Ulysses and Agamemnon arrange false evidence of treason, a letter from Priam and hidden gold, and Palamedes is handed to the allies and stoned to death. His death leads Nauplius to seek revenge on the Greeks.

Nauplius, son of Clymene and father of Palamedes, seeks revenge after Palamedes is killed: denied satisfaction by the Greeks, he arranges adultery among their wives and lights a Mount Caphareus beacon to wreck returning Greeks.
Telemachus, son of Ulysses, learns Ulysses’ identity after his disguised arrival, joins Ulysses, Eumaeus, and Philoetius against the suitors, and helps kill them.

Mycenae was ruled by Agamemnon. Menelaus went there to ask Agamemnon to assemble an army against Troy. Mycenae is where Agamemnon is murdered and where Aegisthus subsequently reigns. Orestes later returns there secretly with Pylades and kills Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra.
Sicyon was ruled by Polyphides, who received the rescued Agamemnon and Menelaus.

Ithaca is an island and Ulysses’s native land. There, he finds his household wasted while suitors pursue Penelope, kills them, and later returns from the land of the Thesprotians to find that Penelope has borne Polypoethes. Telegonus then comes, drives away cattle, and fatally encounters Ulysses defending them.
The text says that Strife threw an apple as a prize of beauty for Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite to contest before Alexander.

The Greek ships assemble at Aulis, reach Mysia while mistakenly thinking it Troy, are scattered by a violent storm, and return home before gathering again. Windlessness holds them at Aulis until Calchas’s demanded sacrifice is arranged. They sail from Tenedos toward Troy and are drawn up after landing. After Troy is plundered, storms founder many ships near Tenos; others are lured by a beacon fire and wrecked at the Capherian rocks.

l: rescue of Agamemnon and Menelaus, The Library
s: takes_to Sicyon The nurse rescued Agamemnon and Menelaus after Atreus’s death by taking them to Polyphides in Sicyon. Polyphides later sent them to Oeneus.

l: marriages of Agamemnon and Menelaus, The Library
s: Agamemnon married Clytaemnestra, daughter of Tyndareus, and Menelaus married Helen. Menelaus received the kingdom of Sparta from Tyndareus.

l: murder of Tantalus and his child, The Library
s: Agamemnon killed Tantalus, the former husband of Clytaemnestra and son of Thyestes, together with Tantalus’s newborn child.
Zeus sent Hermes to bring Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite before Alexander so that he could judge which was fairest. Alexander chose Aphrodite because she promised him Helen.

l: Greek expedition against Troy, The Library
s: After Helen’s abduction, Menelaus asks Agamemnon to organize the Greek expedition against Troy; Agamemnon rallies oath-bound kings. Assembled at Aulis, it mistakenly reaches Mysia, is guided by healed Telephus toward Troy, then is delayed and separated by a storm.

l: raising the Greek army, The Library
s: Agamemnon sent a herald to each of the kings to remind them of their oaths and encourage military support. Many were eager to join the expedition.
Odysseus pretended to be mad because he did not want to join the expedition against Troy. He abandoned the pretense when Palamedes threatened Telemachus.

l: Palamedes’s exposure of Odysseus, The Library
s: Palamedes demonstrated that Odysseus’s madness was false by seizing Telemachus from Penelope and drawing his sword as though he would kill him. Odysseus’s fear for his child made him confess that the madness was feigned.

The Greeks are the forces assembled against Troy. After departing from Aulis, they return there in one account, sail to Tenedos, and then sail to Troy after sending Menelaus and Ulysses to demand Helen’s restoration. When the Trojans refuse, the Greeks land, kill many, confine the Trojans within Troy, and begin a siege. They build a wall and ditch by their ships, but suffer losses, are driven back, and see their ships set on fire before Achilles returns. After ten years they are despondent, then learn from Calchas and Helenus the conditions for taking Troy: they fetch the bones of Pelops, bring Neoptolemus from Scyros, and steal the Palladium. Their best warriors conceal themselves in the Wooden Horse while the rest sail to Tenedos. Returning at night, they enter Troy, kill the sleeping Trojans, burn the city, divide its spoils, and sacrifice to the Greek gods. They decide Astyanax’s death in an assembly according to some accounts. Afterward they quarrel over departure and sacrifice to Athena, leave in separate groups, and endure storms, shipwrecks, and Nauplius’s false lights. Some sail to Mimas, and some settle in Italy.
The letter of treason is written by a Phrygian under compulsion from Odysseus. It is made to appear as though Priam sent it to Palamedes, and Agamemnon reads it in the camp.
Odysseus hides gold in Palamedes's quarters and throws the letter into the camp. Agamemnon finds the gold and treats it as evidence against Palamedes.
The Greek army assembles at Aulis to sail against Troy, ravages Mysia but is driven back by Telephus, and, unable to endure Philoctetes’ wound’s stench, leaves him on Lemnos by Agamemnon’s order.

Aulis is where the Greek army first assembles and later gathers again after eight years. A sacrifice to Apollo takes place there, followed by the serpent omen. ᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] The Greeks arrived at Aulis for the second time, where the fleet was held by windlessness. Iphigenia was brought there and was nearly sacrificed before Artemis carried her away.

inhabit Locris [after regaining their country] The Locrians returned to their country with difficulty and, after a plague struck Locris, received an oracle directing them to propitiate Athena at Ilium. They sent two maidens as suppliants for a thousand years.
is_a place in Thessaly Phylace was the place in Thessaly where the kine were held. Melampus went there, or to Othrys, to obtain them.

emerges_from altar [during a sacrifice to Apollo] A serpent emerges from the altar beside a plane-tree at Aulis. It consumes eight sparrows and their mother, making nine birds, and then turns to stone.

l: prophecy of Troy's capture, The Library
s: foretells Troy [capture after ten years] The prophecy of Troy's capture is given by Calchas after the serpent omen at Aulis. It states that Troy will be captured in ten years.
is_ruled_by Telephus Mysia is mistaken for Troy by the Greeks, who ravage the country. Telephus defends Mysia and drives the Greeks back to their ships.
Son of Heracles and king commanding Mysians against Greeks, Telephus wounds Achilles, is wounded, then comes in rags to be healed and shows Greeks the course to Troy.
Son of Oedipus, husband of Argia, Polynices makes an alternating-rule compact with Eteocles, who refuses Thebes; Polynices kills him in single combat.

is_inflicted_by Achilles [in the thigh with a spear] Telephus's wound is caused when Achilles's spear strikes his thigh as he is pursued in Mysia. The wound remains unhealed until Achilles treats it with rust from the Pelian spear.

l: Apollo's prophecy to Telephus, The Library
s: foretells Telephus's healing [when his assailant becomes his physician] Apollo tells Telephus that he will obtain a cure when the one who wounded him becomes his physician. This prophecy leads Telephus to go to Argos and seek Achilles's help.

l: rust of the Pelian spear, The Library
s: restores Telephus [by healing the wound inflicted by Achilles’s spear] The rust of the Pelian spear is scraped off by Achilles and applied in the healing of Telephus's wound. After being healed, Telephus shows the Greeks the course to Troy.

The course to Troy is unknown to the Greek army after it assembles again at Aulis. Telephus shows it to the Greeks after Achilles heals him, with Calchas confirming the reliability of the guidance through his divination.

Tenes, son of Cycnus and Proclia, though some called him Apollo’s son, was banished by Cycnus in a chest. He settled on Leucophrys, renamed it Tenedos, ruled there, and was killed by Achilles while defending the island.

Cycnus, after having children by Proclia, marries Philonome; believing her false accusation, he casts Tenes and his sister adrift, then kills Philonome and buries her alive on learning the truth, before Achilles kills him.

Tenedos, formerly called Leucophrys and named after Tenes, is an island or offshore anchorage off the Trojan coast. Tenes rules and resists arriving Greeks until Achilles kills him; later Greeks touch there, use it to lie offshore, return to Troy, and Neoptolemus departs after two days.

The Taurians, part of the Scythians, customarily kill strangers by throwing victims into sacred fire; they capture Orestes and Pylades for King Thoas, but Orestes escapes with his sister and the wooden image.

prevents_sailing fleet [according to Calchas] ᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] The windlessness at Aulis prevented the fleet from sailing. Calchas said that it would continue unless Iphigenia was presented as a sacrifice to Artemis.
᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] The oracle declared that the Greeks could not sail unless the fairest of Agamemnon’s daughters was presented as a sacrifice to Artemis.

is_intended_for Artemis [at her altar] ᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] Agamemnon placed Iphigenia beside the altar and was about to slaughter her. Artemis prevented the sacrifice by carrying Iphigenia away.

l: deer substituted for Iphigenia, The Library
s: is_substituted_at altar of Artemis [by Artemis] ᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] Artemis substituted a deer for Iphigenia at the altar after carrying Iphigenia away.

᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] Tenes was banished by Cycnus, who believed Philonome’s false accusation against him, and was set adrift with his sister in a chest. The chest reached Leucophrys, where Tenes settled and founded Tenedos.

᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] Tenes died at Tenedos after Achilles struck him in the breast with a sword. This occurred despite Thetis’s warning that Achilles would die by Apollo’s hand if he killed Tenes.
᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] A water-snake came from the altar during a sacrifice to Apollo and bit Philoctetes.

causes wound of Philoctetes [a non-healing wound] ᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] The snakebite gave Philoctetes a wound that did not heal and became foul-smelling. Because the army could not endure the smell, he was abandoned on Lemnos.

l: abandonment of Philoctetes on Lemnos, The Library
s: takes_place_on Lemnos [by order of Agamemnon] ᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] By Agamemnon’s order, Odysseus abandoned Philoctetes on Lemnos because of the incurable, foul-smelling wound caused by the water-snake. Philoctetes survived in the wilderness by shooting birds with Heracles’ bow.

The Trojans are the inhabitants and defenders of Troy during the Trojan war. They begin by refusing to restore Helen and property, threatening Ulysses and Menelaus, resisting the Greek landing, and being driven back into a besieged city. Joined by allies, they gain confidence when Achilles refuses to fight, drive the Greeks to their wall, breach it, and burn ships, but flee before Patroclus and Achilles. They face further losses from Achilles and Neoptolemus, while Eurypylus defends them and they guard the Palladium. After seeing the Greek camp deserted, they believe the Greeks have fled and drag the Wooden Horse into Troy despite warnings. The Greeks emerge at night, capture the city, defeat the Trojans, and slay them.

l: Greek embassy to Troy, The Library
s: Greek embassy to Troy: Ulysses and Menelaus demand Helen and property; Troy refuses and threatens them, but Antenor saves the envoys.

l: restoration of Helen and the property, The Library
s: The restoration of Helen and the property was demanded by Ulysses and Menelaus. The Trojans refused to grant it, prompting the Greek attack.

l: Greek attack on Troy, The Library
s: is_launched_by Greek forces [after the Trojans’ refusal and threat] The Greek attack on Troy followed the Trojans' refusal to restore Helen and the property. The Greeks landed, drove the barbarians into the city, and began the siege.
Barbarians defend the shore against Greek landing with arms and stones, then flee into Troy after Achilles kills Cycnus.

is_led_by Protesilaus [he is the first Greek to land] The Greek landing was resisted by the barbarians, who threw stones from the shore. Protesilaus was the first Greek to land, and the other Greeks soon leaped from the ships and filled the plain with bodies.

is_caused_by Hector The death of Protesilaus occurred after he was the first Greek to land and had killed many barbarians. Laodamia continued to love him, and Hermes later brought him up from Hades before he was returned there.
Laodamia loves Protesilaus beyond his death, makes his likeness, rejoices when Hermes brings him from Hades, and kills herself after he is taken back.
is_performed_by Achilles [with a stone] The killing of Cycnus was carried out by Achilles with a stone thrown at Cycnus's head. It caused the barbarians to flee into Troy.

The siege of Troy begins when Greek forces drive Trojans into the city, draw up ships, and besiege them; while it keeps Idomeneus from Crete, Leucus debauches Meda, murders her and her daughter, and seizes power.
Allied forces from surrounding cities arrive after nine years, joining Trojans under numerous named leaders, from Aeneas through Sarpedon and Glaucus.
Zeus's son, Lycian leader and king, fights among Trojan allies and is reported killed by Hector or Patroclus.
is_made_or_brought_by Hephaestus Achilles’ arms were set up as a prize for the bravest after his death. They were awarded to Odysseus rather than Ajax.
Chryses’ daughter, captured at Lyrnessus and Achilles’ concubine, causes his refusal to fight until Greeks return her after his anger ends.

Penthesilia, daughter of Otrere and Ares, accidentally kills Hippolyte and is purified by Priam. In battle at Troy she kills many, including Machaon, before Achilles kills her; afterward Achilles falls in love with her and kills Thersites for mocking him.

pursue Orestes [because of his matricide] The Furies pursue Orestes after he kills his mother and Aegisthus. He is later tried at the Areopagus, where he is acquitted when the votes are equal; the Furies are among those said to have brought him to trial.
contains Achilles [as the place where he is buried with Patroclus] The White Isle was the place where Achilles was buried with Patroclus, with their bones mixed together.
After Priam purified Penthesilia, a battle took place in which she killed many people, including Machaon, before Achilles killed her.

is_caused_by Achilles [after her battle at Troy] Penthesilia was killed by Achilles after she had killed many in battle. Achilles fell in love with her after her death and killed Thersites for jeering at him.

l: arrival of Memnon at Troy, The Library
s: involves Memnon [with a great force of Ethiopians] Memnon arrived at Troy with a great force of Ethiopians to fight against the Greeks. He killed many Greeks, including Antilochus, before Achilles killed him.
Achilles was shot in the ankle by Alexander and Apollo at the Scaean gate. He was buried with Patroclus in the White Isle, and games were held in his honour.

l: contest for Achilles' arms, The Library
s: Achilles’ arms were offered as a prize to the bravest, and Ajax and Odysseus competed for them. The Trojans, or according to some the allies, judged the contest and awarded victory to Odysseus.

After losing the contest for Achilles’ arms, Ajax became disturbed with grief and planned a nighttime attack on the army. Athena drove him mad, and after he recovered his senses from slaughtering cattle and their herdsmen, he killed himself.

l: bow and arrows of Hercules, The Library
s: Calchas said that the Greeks could not take Troy unless they had the bow and arrows of Hercules fighting on their side.
protect Troy Helenus was said to know the oracles that protected Troy. Under compulsion, he revealed the conditions for taking Ilium.
The Greeks caused the bones of Pelops to be brought to them as one of the conditions for taking Ilium.
is_ruled_by Lycomedes Odysseus and Phoenix went to Scyros and persuaded Lycomedes to let Neoptolemus go to the Greek camp.
Odysseus entered the Trojan city at night in disguise as a beggar. With Helen's help, he stole the Palladium and, after killing many guards, carried it to the ships with Diomedes.

The Wooden Horse, invented by Ulysses and constructed by Epeus, is a hollow, side-opened supposed sacred offering dedicated to Athena. Ulysses and fifty others hide inside; Trojans drag it into Troy beside Priam’s palace, then the Greeks emerge and destroy the city.

l: Greek expedition to Lemnos, The Library
s: Odysseus and Diomedes undertook the expedition to Lemnos to obtain the bow and arrows of Hercules from Philoctetes.
Philoctetes was healed by Podalirius after arriving at Troy.
Alexander died after Philoctetes shot him with the bow and arrows of Hercules.
Odysseus waylaid and captured Helenus and brought him to the Greek camp. Helenus was then forced to reveal how Ilium could be taken.

l: theft of the Palladium, The Library
s: is_carried_out_by Odysseus [with Helen’s help and Diomedes’ assistance] Odysseus and Diomedes entered the Trojan city at night, stole the Palladium with Helen's help, killed many of its guards, and carried it to the ships.
Eurypylus was killed by Neoptolemus after arriving with a large Mysian force to aid the Trojans.
Sinon, a Greek signal-bearer left behind after the Greeks sail away, lights a beacon from Achilles’ tomb to signal their approach from Tenedos.
Laocoon, described as a seer, also warns that the Wooden Horse contains an armed force. Apollo sends two serpents from nearby islands, and they devour Laocoon’s sons.

The sack of Ilium is the fall of Troy after Greeks use the Wooden Horse to enter and open the gates. Greeks kill sleeping inhabitants, burn the city, divide its spoil, kill Priam and Astyanax, sacrifice Polyxena, and carry away captives including Helen.
Astyanax is killed after Troy’s capture, thrown from the battlements or a high tower. Accounts differ over whether Ulysses or Neoptolemus kills him; Apollodorus regards the death as a sacrifice.

Earth, mother of Titans, is initially described as lacking fire until it is brought or returned, allowing people to cook and make fire. It is later threatened by uncontrolled solar journeys that burn, boil, crack, and kill many people.

The two Locrian maidens took refuge in the sanctuary after being pursued by the inhabitants of Troy. They did not approach Athena, but swept and sprinkled the sanctuary, remained inside it, wore single garments, and had cropped hair.
The sacrifice of Polyxena took place on the grave of Achilles. The notes give traditions in which Achilles’ ghost demanded the sacrifice and in which Neoptolemus performed it.

Astyanax’s death is described as a fall from the battlements. The notes preserve differing accounts naming Ulysses or Neoptolemus as the agent and differing accounts about whether the killing occurred during the sack or afterward by decree.
Achilles’ grave was the site of Polyxena’s slaughter.

is_associated_with Hecate [the fable may have originated in the resemblance of their names] Hecuba’s transformation into a bitch is reported as an alternative tradition. In that account, Helenus took her to the Chersonese, where she was buried at the Bitch’s Tomb.

Mopsus is a diviner, son of Apollo and Manto. At Colophon he received Calchas and companions, prevailed in a dispute about divination by correctly predicting figs and piglets, and later received storm-driven Amphilochus. Fighting Amphilochus in single combat for the kingdom, they killed each other according to one account.

l: storm against the Greeks, The Library
s: A storm sent by Zeus at Athena’s request strikes Greeks near Tenos, founders many ships, and separates Menelaus from the others.

has_alternate_name Caphareus/Xylophagus [the mountain is now called Xylophagus] Nauplius lit a beacon fire on Mount Caphareus, which was also called Xylophagus, to deceive returning Greek ships into approaching the shore as though it were a harbour.

l: shipwreck of the Greeks at Caphereus, The Library
s: During the return from Troy, Greek ships mistake a beacon for a harbour, wreck at Caphereus, and many Greeks die.
Nauplius lit a beacon fire on Mount Caphareus to make the returning Greeks believe that a harbour was nearby. The Greeks approached it and were wrecked on the Capherian rocks.
are_conquered_by Neoptolemus [in battle] The Molossians were defeated by Neoptolemus in battle, after which he became their king.
Molossia was the country to which Neoptolemus traveled by land with Helenus. Helenus founded a city there, and Neoptolemus ruled the Molossians there as king.
A Phocian who kills Neoptolemus after Neoptolemus plunders Apollo’s offerings and burns Delphi’s temple.
Peleus was expelled from Phthia by the sons of Acastus and subsequently died. Neoptolemus then succeeded to his father’s kingdom.

l: Neoptolemus’s journey to Molossia, The Library
s: After remaining in Tenedos for two days on Thetis’s advice, Neoptolemus traveled by land to Molossia with Helenus. Phoenix died along the way, and Neoptolemus buried him.

l: Neoptolemus’s conquest of Molossia, The Library
s: establishes_rule_over Molossians [after victory in battle] Neoptolemus defeated the Molossians in battle and became their king.

l: marriage of Neoptolemus and Hermione, The Library
s: follows Hermione [after her prior betrothal to Neoptolemus in Troy] Neoptolemus took Hermione, who had previously been betrothed to him in Troy, from Orestes when Orestes went mad.

l: Neoptolemus’s death at Delphi, The Library
s: Neoptolemus was killed at Delphi, according to the main account, by Orestes. Another account says that Machaereus killed him after he demanded satisfaction from Apollo, plundered the votive offerings, and burned the temple.

use fire as a means of rejuvenation [by roasting babies to prolong life or render them immortal] After their wanderings and shipwrecks, the Greeks settled in Libya, Italy, Sicily, the islands near Iberia, along the Sangarius River, Cyprus, Crete, and other places. Some Greeks who lost their ships after the Trojan War settled in Italy with the daughters of Laomedon.
Italy, said to be named after a bull, receives Greek refugees including Philoctetes at Crimissa; Greeks and Campanians settle there, with Campania and the river Navaethus noted.

l: Antiphus son of Thessalus, The Library
s: Antiphus went to the Pelasgians, took possession of their country, settled among them, and named it Thessaly.
Phyllis, daughter of the Bisaltians’ king, marries Demophon in love; when he fails to return on time, she curses him and kills herself.

l: casket of Mother Rhea, The Library
s: contain sacrament of Mother Rhea [according to Phyllis] Phyllis gave Demophon the casket of Mother Rhea and told him not to open it until he had abandoned hope of returning to her. When Demophon opened it, he was seized by fear and died while riding.
Locris was afflicted by a plague three years after the Locrians regained their country. The Locrians then sent maidens to Troy in accordance with an oracle.

affect Locris [three years after the Locrians returned] The plague occurred in Locris three years after the Locrians returned there. It led the Locrians to seek an oracle and send two maidens to Athena at Ilium.

l: Locrian maidens sent to Troy, The Library
s: Locrian maidens were sent to Troy in pairs as suppliants to serve and remain within Athena’s sanctuary at Ilium. Beginning with Periboea and Cleopatra, replacements followed after deaths; later infants with nurses were sent, until the practice ended after a thousand years.
At Mycenae, Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra murder Agamemnon; Orestes later takes vengeance on those responsible.
is_a son of Strophius Pylades is the son of Strophius and is raised with Orestes. He accompanies Orestes to Mycenae and to the Taurians, and later marries Electra.

l: oracle concerning Orestes’ vengeance, The Library
s: A divine oracle authorizes Orestes to avenge Agamemnon’s murderers, then directs him to retrieve the Taurian wooden image to end his disorder.

l: vengeance against Agamemnon’s murderers, The Library
s: Orestes’s vengeance: secretly returning to Mycenae with Pylades, killing Clytaemnestra and Aegisthus, then suffering madness and Furies’ pursuit.

A wooden image in the land of the Taurians is sought by Orestes on divine instruction to free him from disorder. He carries it away with Iphigenia to Athens, where it is called Artemis Tauropolus; some place it on Rhodes.
Maron, Apollo’s priest, is spared by Odysseus at Ismarus and gives him wine later used against Polyphemus.

Polyphemus is a huge, wild, man-eating Cyclops and giant, said to be the son of Poseidon and the nymph Thoosa. He has one eye on his forehead, lives in a giant’s cave, and has a thousand sheep. In the Homeric story, he eats some of Odysseus’s companions. Ulysses deceives him by calling himself “Nobody,” blinds him, and escapes; after learning Ulysses’s name, Polyphemus throws rocks at the departing ship. Accounts differ: the Dolopathos narrative calls its giant blear-eyed and has episodes unlike the Odyssey, while other discussions present Polyphemus as the comparable one-eyed cave giant. His story is repeatedly linked with Finnish, Karelian, Lithuanian, German, Yorkshire, Breton, Esthonian, Lapp, and Russian tales. He is treated as a fairyland being; Wilhelm Grimm interprets him as the sun, though another text rejects physical or moral interpretations.

Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe, learns his parentage from Circe and sails to Ithaca seeking Odysseus. After driving away cattle, he wounds Odysseus with a sting-ray-spined spear, then recognizes him, laments, takes Odysseus’s body and Penelope to Circe, marries Penelope, and is sent with her to the Islands of the Blest.

Tiresias is a blind Theban soothsayer, son of Everes and Chariclo and father of Manto, whose sight is lost and whose sex changes repeatedly. He advises the Thebans to sacrifice a human being and abandon their city. After death, Ulysses consults and sacrifices to him; Tiresias directs Ulysses to propitiate Poseidon.

l: land of the Cyclopes, The Library
s: Odysseus reaches the land of the Cyclopes with one ship after leaving the other ships at a neighboring island. He enters Polyphemus's cave there and later escapes by sea.
Polyphemus's cave is near the sea and contains his flocks. Odysseus and twelve companions enter it, become trapped by a huge stone, and escape only after Odysseus blinds Polyphemus.
is_inhabited_by Circe The Aeaean isle is inhabited by Circe. Odysseus reaches it with the one ship that survives the attack of the Laestrygones.
Odysseus’s companions taste lotus and are dragged back; some are eaten by Polyphemus or swept away; twenty-two are transformed and restored by Circe, later use wax and slaughter the Sun’s cattle.

Odysseus initially sails with several ships, leaving the others at a neighboring island before approaching the land of the Cyclopes with one ship. The remaining ships are later destroyed by the Laestrygones, leaving only one to reach the Aeaean isle.

Odysseus wanders from Ilium through Ismarus, the land of the Lotus-eaters, the land of the Cyclopes, Aeolia, the land of the Laestrygones, and the Aeaean isle. The text also says that some accounts place his wandering in Libya, Sicily, the Ocean, or the Tyrrhenian Sea.

is_caused_by Odysseus Odysseus and four companions sharpen and heat a club, then use it to blind Polyphemus while he sleeps after drinking Maron's wine. Odysseus and his companions escape beneath the sheep.

l: shipwreck of Odysseus's fleet, The Library
s: is_caused_by Laestrygones [the rest of the fleet is destroyed] The Laestrygones throw rocks at Odysseus's ships, breaking them and eating their crews. Odysseus cuts the cable of his own ship and escapes, while the other ships and their crews perish.

l: transformation of Odysseus's companions, The Library
s: is_caused_by Circe [through enchantments] Circe mixes an enchantment into a drink of cheese, honey, barley meal, and wine. After the companions drink, she touches them with a wand and changes them into wolves, swine, asses, and lions, but later restores them.

Sirens are bird-shaped women from the thighs downward, daughters of Achelous and Melpomene, comprising Pisinoe, Aglaope, and Thelxiepia. Through lyre, song, and flute, they persuade passing mariners to linger; according to prophecy, they die when a ship passes them.
are_a_route sea passage [one of two ways after the Sirens] The Wandering Rocks lie on one side of the route after the Sirens. By Circe’s advice, Ulysses avoids passing between them.
Charybdis is a sea monster dwelling in a cliff, drawing up and releasing water three times daily; after Ulysses’s ship is destroyed, she swallows its mast, from which he survives.
is_a island of the Sun Thrinacia is the island of the Sun where cattle graze. Ulysses is detained there by lack of wind, and his companions slaughter some of the cattle for food.
is_a island Ogygia is the island to which Ulysses is carried after escaping Charybdis. Calypso receives him there.
Calypso, Atlas’s daughter and a Nereid, receives Ulysses on Ogygia, bears Latinus by him, and is left after five years when he sails away.

receive Ulysses [after he is washed ashore] The Phaeacians receive Ulysses after Poseidon’s anger breaks apart his raft. Alcinous entertains him, gives him gifts, and sends him with a convoy to his native land.
Polyidus, a seer, learns a magical herb’s power from a serpent and uses it to restore the dead Glaucus to life.
Twenty-three Ithacan suitors from Same woo Penelope, consume Ulysses’s herds in palace feasts, and press her to marry; after failing to bend Ulysses’s bow, they are killed by Ulysses and his allies.

is_a servant of Ulysses Eumaeus receives Ulysses when he arrives disguised as a beggar. Ulysses reveals himself to him, and Eumaeus helps Ulysses, Philoetius, and Telemachus plot against and kill the suitors.
Received from Iphitus, Ulysses’ bow tests Penelope’s suitors: none can bend it; Ulysses takes it and shoots them.
Thesprotians receive Ulysses after Epirus and, led by Odysseus against Brygians, their queen Callidice offers him the kingdom.
Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, asks Ulysses to remain and gives him the kingdom. She bears him a son, Polypoetes; after she dies, Ulysses gives the kingdom to their son and returns to Ithaca.

ends_in Ithaca [after his travels] Ulysses returns to Ithaca after being sent home by the Phaeacians and finds his household consumed by the suitors. He disguises himself as a beggar, reunites with Telemachus, kills the suitors, and is recognized by Penelope and Laertes. He later returns again after leaving the Thesprotians.

l: slaughter of the suitors, The Library
s: is_carried_out_by Ulysses [with Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Telemachus] Ulysses carries out the slaughter of the suitors with Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Telemachus after winning the contest of the bow. He also kills Melanthius and the handmaids who had slept with the suitors.

deceives suitors [until it is discovered] Penelope promises to marry after finishing Laertes’s shroud. She weaves it by day and undoes it by night for three years, deceiving the suitors until they discover what she is doing.

l: wound inflicted by the sting-ray, The Library
s: The wound was inflicted by a spear whose point was fitted with the spine of a sting-ray. The wound killed Odysseus.
Odysseus died after Telegonus wounded him while he was defending cattle in Ithaca. Telegonus later recognized him and lamented his death.

contains the Ulysses and Polyphemus story [the Homeric account] The Odyssey contains the well-known account of Ulysses and Polyphemus. The Dolopathos narrative differs from it in the giant's condition, the method of blinding, and the addition of the magic-ring episode.

l: passing newborn infants across fire, The Library
s: An appendix entry describes passing newborn infants across fire as an ancient Greek custom meant to protect them from infancy’s dangers, understood as demons or spiritual beings, alongside carrying children over hearths, through smoke, or around fire.

l: War of Earth on Heaven, The Library
s: The War of Earth on Heaven is a North-Western American Indian tradition story, listed as an appendix heading, in which animals or other Earth people ascend to attack Sky people; versions explain animal traits, stars, and varying causes of the conflict.

Origin of fire is an appendix entry accounted for by Mason-Wasp in the Ba-ila tale and including fire theft as a recurring mythic pattern. It begins with the Ba-ila link between domestic fire and Mason-Wasp construction near fireplaces, includes the Basongo Meno account of fire produced by boring a Raphia-palm rib, and ranges across accounts of humans obtaining fire from gods, animals, birds, or underground guardians.

l: Melampus and the kine of Phylacus, The Library
s: An appendix story of Melampus recovering Phylacus’s kine so Bias can marry Pero, through imprisonment, prophecy, bird consultation, and curing Iphiclus’s childlessness.

Melampus is a soothsayer and son of Amythaon, brother of Bias. Given prophetic powers by snakes, he learns animals’ language. He accepts a year’s imprisonment to win Phylacus’s kine for Bias, cures Iphiclus through prophecy and birds, brings the kine for Pero, later heals Argive women and receives part of Argos.
The kine, originally Tyro's, are stolen by Iphiclus or Phylacus, then recovered by Melampus and brought to Neleus as Pero's bridal gift.

Phylacus, son of Deion by Diomede and father of Iphiclus, is associated in some accounts with possession of kine and reporting Melampus’s escape. When Iphiclus was a child, Phylacus pursued him with a knife and lodged it in a wild pear-tree, said to cause Iphiclus’s childlessness.

Listed as the fifth appendix heading, the Clashing Rocks are Greek-mythology rock formations and a folk-tale motif: two cliffs clash and separate, barely letting a hero or messenger pass, regarded as story-teller’s invention rather than solar myth or icebergs.

l: Phaethon and the chariot of the Sun, The Library
s: is_a appendix entry It is listed as the eleventh appendix heading.
The Sun’s chariot, belonging to the Sun and drawn by fire-breathing horses, normally follows a prescribed course; driven by Phaethon, it runs wildly and causes celestial and earthly destruction.
is_a appendix entry It is listed as the twelfth appendix heading.

An ancient writer recounts Celeus and Metanira's child Demophon, distinct from Triptolemus; after Metanira interrupts Demeter, Demeter angrily throws him down, leaving his survival or death unspecified.

Triptolemus, in accounts identifying him with the fire child, is a child of Celeus. Distinguished from Demophon by some writers, he survives and receives Demeter’s mission to reveal corn to mankind, sowing wheat across the whole earth.

l: infant son of Celeus, The Library
s: The infant son of Celeus is the child whom Demeter is said to have placed on the fire in an attempt to make him immortal. The sources disagree over whether he was Demophon or Triptolemus, who interrupted the rite, and whether he died.

Greek fire-passing customs protect against evil spirits: by the fifth or seventh day after birth, a child was run round the hearth, possibly replacing an older practice of passing the child over fire in houses suggested to have central fireplaces.

identifies_child_as fairy changeling [when a child becomes cross and begins to dwine] The fairy changeling belief held that a sick, wasting, unusually crying, or otherwise troublesome child might be a fairy substitute. In parts of Scotland and Scandinavia, people were said to place or pretend to place such a child over a fire, in an oven, on a gridiron, or in a basket so that the fairy would take it away and return the human child.

threaten newborn infants [according to the rationale of the customs described] Evil spirits are described as dangers believed to threaten newborn infants and their mothers. Fire, smoke, incense, and scented wood are used in various customs to repel, frustrate, or purify against them.

has_region Highlands of Scotland In the Scottish Highlands and islands, children were passed across hearth fires, carried around fires, or swung through smoke to protect them from evil spirits, evil eyes, or illness. In the north-east of Scotland and Fife, fire was also associated with testing or removing fairy changelings, and these customs continued in some places into the nineteenth century.

l: Pend’ d’Oreille Indians of Montana, The Library
s: tell War of Earth on Heaven [in a version of the story] The Pend’ d’Oreille Indians of Montana tell of Earth people led by Grizzly-Bear who make war on the Sky people. In their version, Wren’s arrow begins a chain to the sky, the Earth people are eventually defeated, and many animals are killed or transformed into stars.

Earth people are animals, birds, or fish who make war on Sky people, ascending by a chain of arrows; they win an initial battle, then are routed, killed, stranded in the sky, or transformed into stars.

The Sky people are attacked by the Earth people after the latter reach heaven. Although they initially suffer defeat in some versions, they gather in greater numbers, rout the Earth people, and sometimes transform those left above into stars.

is_a chief [of the Earth people] Grizzly-Bear leads the Earth people in the Pend’ d’Oreille version and orders the warriors to shoot at the moon or sky. He climbs last because of his weight, causing the arrow chain to break, and in the Sanpoil version he again breaks the chain by trying to climb it.

Coyote is an animal repeatedly described as a helper or thief who brings fire to people. It steals fire from Spider’s house, carries a lit cedar brand tied to its tail, becomes exhausted, and passes the fire to bat; across accounts it leads, steals, carries, and organizes fire’s transfer to humans.
Wren, the smallest bird in the Shuswap version, seems too small and weak, yet shoots arrows into the sky; successive arrows form a chain for Earth people to ascend.

forms chain of arrows [when successive arrows lodge in preceding notches] Most arrows shot by the Earth people fall short of the sky. Wren, or Chickadee in some versions, shoots an arrow that sticks in the sky, allowing later arrows to join it.

A chain of arrows forms as each arrow sticks in the preceding arrow’s notch, creating a ladder from earth to sky. In one account it is shaken into a rope. It can break or be knocked down, stranding beings above or making them fall.

has wings [because he spread his robe while falling] Flying-Squirrel spreads a small robe like wings when jumping from the sky. He lands without injury, and the story says this is why he now has something like wings.
Sucker, an animal, jumps unprepared from the sky, breaks bones scattered through its flesh, and in some versions is revived by Tcel.

tell War of Earth on Heaven [in a parallel version] The Okanagon tribe tells that animals, birds, fish, snakes, and toads shoot at the sky, but only Chickadee succeeds. The version includes the fall of the animals, with fish suffering especially badly because they have no wings.
Chickadee, a small bird, succeeds where other animals fail, shooting arrows into the sky until they form a chain for animals to climb.

Among the Nootkas, masks and images of fish were placed near the twins' hut to invite fish to come and be friendly to them. The fish were believed to come in great numbers, contributing to the expectation of a good catch.

tell War of Earth on Heaven [in British Columbia] The Shuswap tribe tells of Black Bear and Wolverene leading fish and birds in an expedition against the Sky people. In their version, the chain is knocked down when the two chiefs quarrel, and the falling animals acquire various bodily peculiarities.

The Quinault Indians tell that Raven’s daughters are taken into the sky, prompting the Earth people to attack in order to recover one of them. Their version includes Wren’s arrow chain, Beaver’s theft of fire, the cutting of the Sky people’s fastenings, and the eventual retreat when the chain breaks.

Raven is a fire-bringer who steals fire: among the Chilcotin Indians, he lights pitchwood shavings in his hair and kindles fires throughout the country; among the Haida Indians, he takes a burning brand and spreads fire in flight; and he returns from an island with a half-burnt bill. He can wear or remove feathers and appear as a spruce fir leaf. As father of two daughters, he gathers people and animals to attack Sky people after one dies descending.

Raven’s younger daughter, longing to join a bright star, is taken to the sky and finds a feeble old man. She borrows Spider’s rope to descend, but it falls short of earth, leaving her suspended above her father’s house until she dies.

is_a daughter of Raven [elder daughter] Raven’s elder daughter wishes to be with a little star and finds that her star is a young man. She is found in a Sky person’s house and is taken back by the Earth people during their retreat.

spins thread [in the Loango origin account] In Loango, the spider spun a long thread whose end the wind carried to the sky, allowing the woodpecker and then man to climb up and bring down fire. Among the Sia Indians, Spider created men and animals, made fire underground, and guarded it with a snake, cougar, and bear.

Beaver is an animal among the Earth People and a thief of fire in several versions. After Robin Redbreast, Dog, and Wildcat fail, Beaver obtains fire for the Earth People from the Sky People. In other tellings, Eagle, sometimes Weasel, assists Beaver, who steals glowing coals by feigning death in a fish trap and escapes with fire in a clam-shell or hidden under his skin.
A bird climbs the spider’s thread to the sky and pecks the celestial vault, making stars; afterward man follows and fetches fire from the sky.

inhabit interior of British Columbia The Thompson Indians, who inhabit the interior of British Columbia, tell versions of a fire-theft myth involving Coyote, Beaver, Eagle, and Weasel. In one version Beaver steals fire in a clam-shell while Eagle diverts the attention of its owners.

l: the Greek myth of the origin of fire, The Library
s: features fire [as stolen from a deity or fairyland being] The Greek myth explains the arrival of fire among men through Prometheus’s theft. The fire is variously said to come from Zeus himself or from the workshop of Hephaestus and Athena, and it may also be associated with Hephaestus’s fall from heaven to Lemnos.

Men receive fire from Prometheus in Greek accounts and from birds, animals, heroes, insects, or spirits in other traditions. They use it for cooking and learn methods of making it by observing or acquiring the secrets of supernatural beings.

Māui is a great primordial hero in Maori and other Polynesian traditions who obtains fire for earth from Mahuika, sometimes as a bird, and in one Hawaiian account learns fire-making from an alae bird.

is_a goddess of fire [and Māui's grandmother] Mahuika is the Maori goddess of fire and the source from whom Māui obtains fire. At his request, she produces fire successively from the nails of her fingers and toes, after which a great conflagration occurs and the surviving fire takes refuge in trees.
Ba-ila inhabit Northern Rhodesia in Central Africa and have an account of Ngongwa becoming a Mason-Wasp, explaining fireplaces and domestic fire.

Mason-Wasp, common in Central Africa and called Ngongwa, is a winged, yellow-abdomened, black-and-orange-legged creature regarded as the Ba-ila’s Prometheus, bringing fire from God. It builds and seals mud cells on fireplaces, houses, walls, books, and pictures, lays eggs with grubs, and its young eat insects benumbed by stinging. Ngongwa is supposed to change into it.

Fire-making by friction is a method of producing fire with wood by boring or rubbing. Stories describe it being learned through observation or instruction, including watching gods, spirits, birds, or insects. The Basongo Meno use a pointed stick to bore a Raphia-palm rib, a practice employed since fire was first elicited this way.
Ngongwa is a child placed in a dwelling near a fireplace for many days, then supposed to metamorphose into a Mason-Wasp.
Basongo Meno are a group of tribes in the Congo basin, north of the Sankuru and Kasai rivers. They make fishing-traps from Raphia palm ribs and say fire was first produced while a man made one.
The Congo basin is identified as the region containing the territory of the Basongo Meno.
is_maintained_in plantation [to supply fire-sticks] The Basongo Meno make fishing-traps from the ribs of the Raphia palm. They maintain large plantations of Raphia palm to supply fire-sticks.
